readerTitle: Why a $20 ramen bowl that few people order still pays off
caseNote: 가상 사례 (라멘 가게, 프로젝트 관리 소프트웨어) + 일반 관찰 (주유소 연료 등급, 항공 좌석 등급) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가격이 하나뿐이면 더 낼 사람과 덜 낼 사람을 모두 놓친다. 단계를 나누면 고객이 스스로 자기 가격을 고른다.
misconception: 싼 등급을 만들면 기존 고객이 내려가서 손해다. 비싼 등급은 사는 사람이 적으면 실패다.

sources.text: 가격 전략의 일반 개념 (good-better-best, 단계별 가격, 등급 간 차이를 두는 장치)
모든 라멘 가게·소프트웨어 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Watch out 카드: 하향 50명일 때 Basic 70 × $7 = $490, Standard 30 × $10 = $300, Deluxe $280, 합계 $1,070 (+$70). 계산 재확인 필요.
주유소 연료 등급(regular, mid-grade, premium)과 항공 좌석 등급(economy, premium economy, business)은 일반적 관찰로만 언급했습니다. 구체적 가격이나 판매 비중은 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why a $20 ramen bowl that few people order still pays off
body: A ramen shop sells one bowl at $14. About 100 people order it each day.
Some of them would gladly pay more for extra toppings. Others glance at the menu and walk on. One price serves the middle and misses both ends.

image.label: One ramen bowl, with customers walking past on both sides
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 라멘 가게 앞 메뉴판에 "Ramen $14" 하나만 적혀 있음. 한쪽엔 더 비싼 걸 찾는 듯한 손님, 다른 쪽엔 가격을 보고 돌아서는 손님. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Only 1 in 5 orders the deluxe bowl.
body: The owner adds a $20 deluxe bowl with extra pork, egg and a larger portion. It costs $6 to make, versus $4 for the regular.
After a month, about 20 of the 100 regular customers order it each day. The rest still order the $14 bowl. Was the deluxe bowl worth adding?

options.text: No. Too few people order it, so drop it and simplify the menu
options.feedback: A simpler menu is nice, but you'd give up money from people who already wanted to pay more. Low volume doesn't mean low value.

options.text: Yes. Each deluxe bowl leaves $4 more than a regular one
options.feedback: Right. $20 − $6 = $14 left, versus $10 on a regular bowl. Twenty upgrades add $80 a day from customers you already had.

options.text: Only if it makes the $14 bowl look cheap by comparison
options.feedback: That effect can be real, but it's a bonus. The deluxe bowl pays its own way even if nobody's view of the $14 bowl changes.

cards.title: Now add a $10 basic bowl too.
body: The basic bowl costs $3 to make. It brings in 20 new customers who skipped the $14 bowl. But 15 regulars trade down to it.
Daily earnings after ingredients rise from $1,000 to **$1,175**. The trade-downs cost $45. The new customers bring $140.

cards.title: Good, better, best
body: **Good, better, best** means offering the same core product at three levels, so each customer picks the price that fits them.
With one price, you lose twice. People who would pay more pay only $14. People who would pay $10 pay nothing, because they leave.
Three levels let customers sort themselves. You don't have to guess who is who.

image.label: Three bowls in a row: small, regular, loaded
image.brief: 세 그릇을 나란히. 왼쪽 "Good $10" 단출한 그릇, 가운데 "Better $14", 오른쪽 "Best $20" 토핑이 가득한 그릇. 각 그릇 아래 작은 손님 아이콘이 스스로 줄을 선 모습.

cards.title: The gaps between tiers do the work.
body: Tiers only work if they differ in something some customers care about a lot and others barely notice. Extra toppings matter to a hungry regular, not to a student on a budget.
You see this everywhere: regular, mid-grade and premium fuel. Economy, premium economy and business class. Each step adds something a certain group values.
cards.softwareNote: Software plans often separate tiers by features big customers need and small ones don't, such as admin controls, security reviews or faster support. A solo user never misses them. A large company can't buy without them.

cards.title: A basic tier that's too good eats your middle.
body: If the $10 bowl were nearly as filling as the $14 one, far more regulars would trade down. With 50 trade-downs instead of 15, the daily gain shrinks from $175 to **$70**.
The cheap tier must be good enough to buy, but clearly missing something. Tiers also add work: more prep, more choices to explain. Three levels usually beat seven.

cards.title: Now it's a project management app.
body: Your app has one plan: $30 per team per month. Small teams say it's too pricey. Large companies ask for admin controls and phone support. Which set of tiers fits best?

options.text: $15 with every feature, $30 adds priority email, $60 adds a fancier name
options.feedback: The $15 plan gives away almost everything, so many current teams would drop to it. And the $60 plan offers nothing big buyers asked for.

options.text: $15 with core features and 3 projects, $30 as today, $60 adds admin controls and phone support
options.feedback: Small teams get a way in, current users have little reason to drop down, and large customers pay for what they actually need.

options.text: Keep $30 and add only a $60 plan for large companies
options.feedback: You capture more from big buyers, but the small teams who find $30 too much still walk away.

cards.title: Let customers choose their own price.
body: One price serves the middle and loses both ends. Three well-separated levels catch those who want more and those who want less.
**Try it today:** take your main product. Write down what you could remove for a cheaper version and what you could add for a premium one. Who would pick each?
